newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin recovering well after surgery, doctors say.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin recovering well after surgery, doctors say.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was recovering normally on Thursday after his heart operation and there were no signs of problems, a Kremlin spokesman said.

Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Itar-Tass news agency that doctors had met on Thursday morning to discuss the results of Tuesday's seven-hour operation and concluded they were "positive and there is nothing untoward".

The doctors, who consulted for about 90 minutes at the Cardiology Research Centre where the quintuple bypass operation was carried out, have been delighted with the rapid recovery of the 65-year-old president.

But Yastrzhembsky did not say whether they had granted Yeltsin's request to be moved to a more convenient clinic to convalesce. He also did not make clear if they had seen the patient himself during their consultations.

Yeltsin hopes the surgery, intended to improve the flow of blood to his heart, will allow him to reassert full control in Russia to deal with the economic and political problems that have piled up in his four months out of the Kremlin.
Supporters of the opposition communists were gathering in Moscow and other cities ready to march to commemorate the 79th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.
One of the U.S. doctors who have been in Moscow to monitor Yeltsin's treatment, told Reuters late on Wednesday: "He is doing very well."
"If he continues to progress as well as he has done he could move to another clinic on Thursday," added Professor George Noon of Baylor College of Medicine.

Yeltsin, clearly eager to show to the world the speed of his recovery, has badgered doctors to move him from the intensive care unit at the Cardiology Research Centre to the elite Central Clinical Hospital nearby.

He took back his full presidential powers, including the button that controls Russia's nuclear arsenal, from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday morning, less than 24 hours after surrendering them.
Yeltsin's wife Naina, speaking to Russian television on Wednesday evening, was visibly relieved after seeing her husband half-sitting up in bed and speaking freely.
Naina, who visited Yeltsin with their two daughters, said he would have to be restrained from acting too hastily.
"In my opinion he himself feels better," she said. "We will really, really hold him back."

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, 88, who advised on the seven-hour operation to graft in veins to bypass five blockages in Yeltsin's cardiac arteries, said he could be back on the tennis court in four months.
But the president, a keen sportsman, must be patient and follow doctors' orders, DeBakey added.
Problems awaiting Yeltsin's attention include industrial unrest over unpaid wages, the crisis in breakaway Chechnya and a strong showing by political opponents in regional elections.
Gennady Zyuganov, whose Communist Party dominates the State Duma lower house of parliament, went on the offensive at a rally of the party faithful on Wednesday evening.
"The country is run by thieves and drunkards," he said, standing beneath a giant poster of Lenin and recalling the glory days of the Soviet superpower.
Zyuganov said before Tuesday's operation that the president was too sick to govern and has urged him to resign.
